extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, public finance, and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from an 18th-century political economy treatise setting out normative principles about church government, clergy behaviour, education, and the proper sources and allocation of public revenue. It articulates standards for institutional design and public finance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established episcopal government promotes peace and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that preserve episcopal government, subordination among the clergy, and sovereign disposal of bishoprics tend to be favourable to peace and good order and not occasion civil commotion where once established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sovereign's control over appointments renders him the real head of the church and fosters loyalty; this structure avoids the tumults that popular election of clergy may produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should cultivate elite esteem without neglecting lower ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: Clergy often recommend themselves to sovereigns and gentry by learning, decent manners, social good humour, and contempt of fanatic austerities, but in paying court to patrons they are apt to neglect means of maintaining influence with the lower orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While cultivating patrons through learning and decorum gains esteem among superiors, the same clergy frequently fail to defend their doctrines effectively before common people when neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular election of pastors risks faction and disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving parishioners the right to elect their own pastor tends to produce disorder and confusion, corrupting morals of clergy and people and encouraging fanaticism and factional contests over appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular elections often operate under the influence of factional clergy, lead to almost constant violent contests, and may force magistrates to assume patronage rights to preserve public peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of clerical authority is stabilizing; equality of benefice has mixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Presbyterian equality establishes equality of authority (perfect) and aims at equality of benefice (not fully achieved). Equality of authority is uniformly beneficial; equality of benefice produces mediocrity with some agreeable social effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where benefices are nearly equal and moderate, clergy are more likely to live exemplary morals and have stronger influence over common people; large disparities in benefice invite courtship of patrons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrate assumption of patronage to preserve peace
rubrics_metrics.description: In small republics or cities where ecclesiastical elections threaten public order, magistrates find it necessary to assume rights of presentation to vacant benefices for the sake of public peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional intervention is justified when parish disputes repeatedly generate broader civic factionalism or schisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church may require popular concurrence for ecclesiastical jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where law gives the benefice to the person presented by a patron, the church sometimes requires a concurrence of the people before conferring the cure of souls, delaying settlement until concurrence can be procured for the peace of the parish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is framed as an 'affected concern for the peace of the parish' and can be manipulated by clergy to procure or prevent concurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediocrity of benefice fosters moral exemplary behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: When benefices are moderate and nearly equal, none can be very great; this mediocrity obliges clergy to adopt exemplary morals and modest behaviour, which gains esteem and affection of common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small revenues make levity and vanity ruinous; clergy of modest means are induced to instruct, assist, and refrain from contemptuous airs toward the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative wealth of church affects distribution of learned men
rubrics_metrics.description: Where church benefices are moderate, universities attract the best men of letters; where church benefices are considerable, the church drains universities of eminent scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial incentives shape where intellectual talent resides: generous church preferment draws academics into ecclesiastical careers, impoverishing universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching repeatedly is the most effectual method to master a subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposing the necessity of teaching a subject year after year is an effective way to render a person master of it, because repeated exposition forces familiarity and correction of hasty opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual repetition of lectures leads to deep acquaintance with every part of the subject and encourages correction upon reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expenses benefiting the whole society should be defrayed generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses for defending the society and supporting the dignity of the chief magistrate are laid out for the general benefit and so reasonably defrayed by general contribution of the whole society, proportioned to abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim extends to other public goods whose benefits are societal rather than local.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of justice can be funded by those causing or immediately benefiting
rubrics_metrics.description: While the administration of justice benefits society generally, the persons who give occasion to its expense (wrongdoers) or those most immediately benefited (litigants) may appropriately defray its costs via court fees; general taxation should be a last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only for convicting criminals without estate should general revenue be used; otherwise fees on users/culprits are justifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local or provincial expenses ought to be locally funded
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses whose benefit is confined to a part of society (e.g., police of a town) ought to be defrayed by local or provincial revenue and not be a burden on the general revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unjust for the whole society to contribute toward expenses benefiting only a part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roads and communications: charge immediate users or consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance of roads and communications benefits the whole society but is most immediately beneficial to travellers, carriers, and consumers; tolls (turnpike, peages) appropriately lay these costs on those groups rather than general revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User charges can discharge general revenues from a considerable burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and religious instruction may be publicly funded or privately borne
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions for education and religious instruction benefit society at large and can be defrayed by general contribution; but they might with equal propriety be paid by those who receive immediate benefit or by voluntary contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of funding depends on practicability and potential advantages of beneficiary or voluntary funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: When particular contributions fall short, general revenue must cover public institution deficits
rubrics_metrics.description: If institutions or public works beneficial to all cannot be fully maintained by those most immediately benefited, the general revenue should typically make up the deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General revenue supplements particular contributions to sustain public goods essential for society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of public revenue: stock versus land
rubrics_metrics.description: Public revenue may be drawn from funds peculiar to the sovereign/commonwealth (stock or land) or from the revenue of the people; stock and credit are unstable/perishable while land is a more stable permanent fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stock-derived revenues (profits/interest) are less reliable for a permanent revenue base; rent of public lands has historically been a principal and stable source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments can profit from mercantile projects with caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mercantile projects (post-office, public bank, pawn-shop) can yield public revenue; successful management requires orderly, vigilant, and parsimonious administration — qualities not always present in sovereign governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-office is cited as a reliably managed mercantile project; banks and other ventures may succeed under proper administration but often fail when sovereign profusion or poor agent incentives prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lending public treasure abroad is revenue with contingent security
rubrics_metrics.description: A state may derive revenue by lending treasure (placing funds in foreign public funds), but the security of such revenue depends on the solvency of those funds and continuity of peace with debtor nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In wartime, such foreign funds may be forfeited; therefore lending as revenue is conditional on geopolitical stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuing transferable bills of credit can temporarily fund expenditures if moderate and credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Advancing transferable paper bills of credit redeemable later (legal tender between inhabitants) can raise moderate revenue and defray expenses if used with moderation, good government credit, and sufficient demand for currency; overuse produces disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful use requires the total paper not exceeding what gold/silver would have been necessary; historical American colonial experiments illustrate both success and failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character incompatibility between trader and sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispositions and administrative habits of sovereigns and their agents (profusion, careless management) make princes generally poor merchants; trading spirit and sovereign responsibilities are inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (East India Company, princes engaging in trade) show failures when sovereignty replaces merchant incentives.
